Consult Summary:
- Young woman with 3-day history of new, severe, predominantly right-periorbital headache with photophobia and intermittent “shooting lights”; clinician's working impression is probable migraine but in-person neurological exam and fundoscopy arranged to exclude secondary causes (DDx considerations include migraine, CVST, IIH).

History:
- Presenting complaint:
  - “Blinding” severe headache for 3 days, onset sudden on waking.
  - Pain generalized but worse over the right eye; intensity reported as 8/10 at worst, improving to ~5/10 with ibuprofen.
  - Associated photophobia and intermittent visual phenomena described as “shooting lights.”
  - Reports feeling “a bit sick” but no vomiting.
- Timeline:
  - Started abruptly 3 days ago on waking and has been largely continuous since then.
  - Partial transient relief with ibuprofen; not fully resolving.
  - Sleep generally preserved; headache does not wake patient from sleep but may be present on waking.
  - Missed 1 full day of work (works from home; reduced function today).
- Exacerbating/relieving factors:
  - Slight improvement with ibuprofen; advised that paracetamol can be taken with the new prescription.
  - Occasional stabbing pain when standing up quickly or moving head.
  - Light exposure worsens symptoms (photophobia).
- Associated symptoms / systems review:
  - No vomiting, no fever reported, no neck stiffness.
  - No sensory loss, numbness, weakness, change in smell/taste.
  - No cough, sputum, sinus symptoms, epistaxis, or haemoptysis.
- Pertinent negatives:
  - No prior similar prolonged headaches (past headaches brief and responsive to ibuprofen).
  - No recent travel, no recent head trauma.
  - No vomiting, no loss of consciousness, no focal neurologic symptoms reported.

Past Medical History:
- No chronic medical conditions reported.
- Remote childhood episode of unspecified pain that resolved; no diagnosis or complications documented.

Medications:
- Combined oral contraceptive pill — name not documented; dose/route/frequency not documented.
- Intermittent ibuprofen for headache — dose/route/frequency not documented.
- Advised paracetamol can be taken in addition (dose/route/frequency not documented).
- Allergies: none reported.

Social History:
- Lives alone.
- Occupation: works from home.
- Tobacco: denies smoking.
- Alcohol: drinks approximately once weekly; patient stated “three, once a week” (amount per session unclear).
- Recreational drug use: denies.

Family History:
- Mother has severe migraines with vomiting.
- No other family history documented.

Physical Examination:
- Vitals: Not recorded.
- Examination findings: Not recorded. (Clinician planned neurological examination and fundoscopy at follow-up.)

Investigations:
- None performed or available from this consultation.
- Patient reports a pharmacy blood pressure check ~1 year ago that was said to be normal (no documentation available).
- Plan for in-person neuro exam and fundoscopic exam; consideration of imaging if indicated (see plan).

Assessment & Plan:

- Overall Impression:
  - Working diagnosis: Probable migraine (possible migraine with visual phenomena/aura) — aligns with clinician assessment in transcript. Secondary causes must be excluded given continuous severe headache for 3 days and OCP use.

- DDx Integration (brief):
  - Migraine (probable migraine with visual aura) — supporting: photophobia, visual phenomena (“shooting lights”), severe pain partially responsive to analgesia, family history of migraine; opposing: continuous severe headache for 3 days without clear stereotyped transient aura (DDx ranks this as most likely).
  - Cerebral venous sinus thrombosis (CVST) — supporting: young woman on combined OCP, subacute progressive headache, visual symptoms, positional/stabbing element with movement; opposing: no focal neurological signs or documented papilloedema yet (DDx rates medium likelihood).
  - Idiopathic intracranial hypertension (IIH) — supporting: young woman with persistent headache and visual disturbances; opposing: no documented papilledema, no reported obesity or pulsatile tinnitus, and onset was abrupt (DDx rates medium likelihood).
  - No direct conflict between transcript and DDx (both consider migraine most likely while recommending exclusion of secondary causes).

- Issue 1: Acute severe headache — probable migraine
  - Assessment: Clinical features most consistent with migraine (photophobia, visual phenomena, family history) per clinician impression.
  - Plan:
    - Arrange in-person appointment for full neurological examination and fundoscopy (booked via support team; may be cancelled if symptoms resolve).
    - Prescribe a stronger analgesic than ibuprofen (medication name/dose/route/frequency not documented in transcript) and advise paracetamol may be taken concurrently; instruct patient to take medications with food.
    - Advise usual abortive migraine measures as appropriate (analgesia as prescribed; avoid triggers) — as discussed.
    - Safety-net: go to Emergency Department immediately if headache markedly worsens, becomes unbearable, or if new focal neurological signs, altered consciousness, confusion, vomiting, or visual loss occur.
    - Follow-up: revisit after in-person exam; specialist referral considered if abnormal exam or persistent/recurrent severe headaches.

- Issue 2: Rule out secondary causes (CVST, IIH, SAH and other intracranial pathology)
  - Assessment: Red flags include new severe continuous headache, visual phenomena, and combined OCP use (prothrombotic risk) — secondary causes must be considered.
  - Plan:
    - Perform focused neurological exam and fundoscopy at in-person visit (to look for focal deficits, papilledema).
    - If examination reveals focal neurological deficit, papilledema, worsening symptoms, or clinical concern for CVST/SAH/raised intracranial pressure → arrange urgent neuroimaging (e.g., CT head ± venography or MRI/MRV) and urgent referral to secondary care per local protocols. (Imaging modalities not specified in transcript; these are listed as conditional next steps consistent with DDx.)
    - If exam is normal and symptoms resolve, manage as primary headache and reassess if recurrence or change.

- Issue 3: Combined oral contraceptive (OCP) and headache management
  - Assessment: OCP is a potential thrombotic risk factor relevant to CVST consideration; migraine with aura may influence contraceptive suitability.
  - Plan:
    - Check blood pressure at in-person visit (clinician stated BP will be checked).
    - Continue current OCP for the moment as per clinician; if migraine with aura is confirmed, discuss contraceptive options and change of method as appropriate.
    - Document OCP type later when medication reconciliation is completed.

- General plan items:
  - Provide clear written advice to patient about indications for immediate ED attendance (worsening/unbearable pain, focal deficits, vomiting, altered consciousness, visual loss).
  - Patient to contact support team to book examination; appointment may be cancelled if symptoms settle.
  - Reconcile medication names/doses at in-person visit (currently missing).

Quality checks:
- Missing but clinically expected elements: vital signs, full medication name/dose/route/frequency, in-person neurological and eye exam findings, objective BP measurement, and imaging/lab results (none recorded).
- Conflicts between transcript and DDx: None noted — DDx expands differential consistent with clinician’s plan to examine and exclude secondary causes.
- Transcript quality: Initial audio volume problems noted by clinician; remainder of consultation intelligible with some brief interruptions.
